sections.title: Windows Features and Tools
sections.file: 1.4 Microsoft Windows Operating System Features and Tools.html

sections.title: macOS Features and Tools
sections.file: 1.8 Common Features and Tools of the macOS Desktop Operating System.html

terms.name: Operating System
terms.definition: An operating system is foundational system software that manages a computer’s hardware and software resources while acting as an intermediary between the user, applications, and physical components.

terms.name: Windows
terms.definition: Major market presence. Many different versions, such as Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server.

terms.name: Linux
terms.definition: Free Unix-compatible software system. Unix-like, but not Unix. Many different distributions such as Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat, and Fedora.

terms.name: macOS
terms.definition: A desktop OS running on Apple hardware.

terms.name: Chrome OS
terms.definition: Google’s operating system, based on the Linux kernel. It centers around the Chrome web browser, and most apps are web-based. Many manufacturers make Chromebooks, and devices are relatively less expensive.

terms.name: iPadOS
terms.definition: Operating system for Apple’s iPad tablets and a variant of Apple’s phone OS (iOS).

terms.name: iOS
terms.definition: Apple iOS, used for Apple iPhones, is based on Unix. It is closed source (no public access to the source code) and exclusive to Apple products.

terms.name: Android
terms.definition: Google Android is backed by the Open Handset Alliance. It is an open-source OS based on Linux and is supported on many manufacturers’ devices.

terms.name: File Systems
terms.definition: A file system is the method and data structure an operating system uses to organize, name, store, and retrieve files on a storage device.

terms.name: New Technology File System (NTFS)
terms.definition: Extensive improvements over FAT32: quotas, file compression, encryption, symbolic links, large file support, security, and recoverability.

terms.name: Resilient File System (ReFS)
terms.definition: An update to NTFS concepts for Server 2012 and later, with limited support in Windows 8.1 and later. Built for huge storage requirements and very large drives and storage arrays.

terms.name: File Allocation Table 32 (FAT32)
terms.definition: FAT (File Allocation Table) is one of the first PC-based file systems (circa 1980).

terms.name: Fourth extended filesystem (ext4)
terms.definition: Fourth extended file system — an update to ext3. Commonly seen in Linux and Android OS.

terms.name: Extended filesystem (XFS)
terms.definition: High-performance file system for Linux, supported in most Linux distributions. Designed for scalability, large-scale computing, and high-speed processing.

terms.name: Apple File System (APFS)
terms.definition: Added in macOS High Sierra (10.12.4). Also included with iOS and iPadOS. Optimized for solid-state storage.

terms.name: Extensible File Allocation Table (exFAT)
terms.definition: Microsoft flash drive file system. Files can be larger than 4 gigabytes. Compatible across many operating systems — Windows, Linux, and macOS.

terms.name: End-of-life (EOL)
terms.definition: Vendor-specific limitations. Different companies set their own EOL policies for when a product stops receiving updates and support.

terms.name: Update limitations
terms.definition: iOS, Android, and Windows check and prompt for updates. Chrome OS will update automatically.

terms.name: Compatibility concerns between operating systems
terms.definition: Some movies and music can be shared. However, there is no direct application compatibility. Fortunately, many apps have been built to run on different OSes.

terms.name: GUID
terms.definition: Globally Unique Identifier — a 128-bit value used to uniquely identify partitions, disks, and other objects in modern systems.

terms.name: GPT (GUID Partition Table)
terms.definition: The latest partition format standard. Requires a UEFI BIOS.

terms.name: Master Boot Record (MBR)
terms.definition: Maximum partition size of 2 TB. Maximum of four primary partitions per storage drive. One primary partition can be marked as Active (bootable).

terms.name: Disk Partitioning
terms.definition: First step when preparing disks. The drive may already be partitioned; existing partitions may not always be compatible with your new OS.

terms.name: Partitioning
terms.definition: Separate the physical drive into logical pieces. Useful to keep data separated; multiple partitions are not always necessary.

terms.name: USB
terms.definition: The USB device must be bootable. The computer must support booting from USB.

terms.name: Network — PXE
terms.definition: Perform a remote network installation. The computer must support booting with PXE.

terms.name: Solid-state / flash drives
terms.definition: Store many OS installation files. Often used as the target drive or as installation media depending on the deployment method.

terms.name: Internet-based
terms.definition: Boot or install across the internet. Examples include Linux distributions, macOS Recovery installation, and Windows updates.

terms.name: External / hot-swappable drive
terms.definition: Some external drives can mount an ISO image (optical drive image). Can also boot from USB.

terms.name: Internal hard drive (partition)
terms.definition: Install and boot from separate drives, or create and boot from a new partition on an existing internal drive.

terms.name: Multiboot
terms.definition: Pick from two or more operating systems from a boot menu — Windows, Linux, etc.

terms.name: Clean install
terms.definition: Wipe the slate clean and reinstall. A migration tool can help move data afterward.

terms.name: Upgrade
terms.definition: Maintain existing applications and data while moving to a newer OS version.

terms.name: Image deployment
terms.definition: Deploy a clone on every computer. Relatively quick and can be completely automated.

terms.name: Remote network installation
terms.definition: Install from a local server or shared drive — or across the internet.

terms.name: Zero-touch deployment
terms.definition: An automatic install with streamlined implementation. Customize the installation process and automate the entire workflow.

terms.name: Recovery partition
terms.definition: Hidden partition with installation files used to restore or reinstall the OS without external media.

terms.name: Repair installation
terms.definition: Fix problems with the Windows OS. Does not modify user files.

terms.name: Third-party drivers
terms.definition: Load alternate third-party drivers when necessary — disk controller drivers, storage drivers, etc.

terms.name: Quick format
terms.definition: Creates a new file table. Looks like data is erased, but it is not. No additional checks.

terms.name: Drive format
terms.definition: Determining whether a target drive already contains data, has been formatted, or requires partition setup prior to OS installation.

terms.name: Backup files and user preferences
terms.definition: Preserving important files, personal documents, and user preferences prior to installation or drive wiping.

terms.name: Application and driver support / backward compatibility
terms.definition: Verifying that current applications, documents, and system settings will remain supported and functional when updating the OS.

terms.name: Hardware compatibility
terms.definition: Checking that hardware meets minimum system specifications (memory, disk space) and required hardware security capabilities, such as TPM 2.0 and UEFI Secure Boot.

terms.name: End-of-life (EOL)
terms.definition: Vendor-specific limitations. Different companies set their own EOL policies for when a product stops receiving updates and support.

terms.name: Update limitations
terms.definition: iOS, Android, and Windows check and prompt for updates. Chrome OS will update automatically.

terms.name: Compatibility concerns between operating systems
terms.definition: Some movies and music can be shared. However, there is no direct application compatibility. Fortunately, many apps have been built to run on different OSes.

terms.name: Feature updates
terms.definition: Annual operating system releases that introduce new capabilities, UI features, and system updates.

terms.name: Product life cycle
terms.definition: The period post-release — typically 18 to 36 months depending on the Windows edition — during which an OS version receives security patches and support under the Modern Lifecycle Policy.

terms.name: Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
terms.definition: A dedicated hardware-based security microchip that securely stores cryptographic keys, credentials, and encryption measurements used by features like BitLocker.

terms.name: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI)
terms.definition: Modern motherboard system firmware that replaced legacy BIOS, offering faster boot times, support for large drives, and enhanced startup security features like Secure Boot.

terms.name: Windows 10 Home
terms.definition: Designed for home users and purchased at a retail store. Integration with Microsoft account and OneDrive backup. Includes Windows Defender. You can use Cortana to talk to your OS.

terms.name: Windows 10 Pro
terms.definition: The business version of Windows with additional management features.

terms.name: Windows 10 Pro for Workstations
terms.definition: An edition for high-end desktops with enhanced performance and storage options.

terms.name: Windows 10 Enterprise
terms.definition: Built for large implementations with volume licensing.

terms.name: Windows 11 Home
terms.definition: Designed for home use. Integrated with Microsoft accounts. Can be installed with a local account. Limited management functionality — no support for Active Directory.

terms.name: Windows 11 Pro
terms.definition: Large-scale system management. Integrates with Active Directory (Microsoft’s directory services).

terms.name: Windows 11 Enterprise
terms.definition: Built for large company deployments with volume licensing and server-style management features.

terms.name: N Versions
terms.definition: The result of antitrust investigations by the European Commission. No Windows Media Player included. Media features can be added to Windows later.

terms.name: Domain vs Workgroup
terms.definition: Centralized network management. User accounts and security policies are managed by a central server (Domain Controller).

terms.name: Desktop styles / user interface
terms.definition: The visual presentation, layouts, Start menu behaviors, and taskbar configurations provided by different Windows versions or editions.

terms.name: Availability of Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)
terms.definition: RDP allows a user to remotely control a PC over a network connection.

terms.name: Random-access memory (RAM) support limitations
terms.definition: Physical memory caps built into specific Windows editions and architectures.

terms.name: BitLocker
terms.definition: A full-disk encryption security feature included in Windows Pro, Enterprise, and Education editions that protects drive contents by scrambling data when the system is offline or powered down.

terms.name: gpedit.msc
terms.definition: The Local Group Policy Editor console, available in Pro and higher editions, used by administrators to configure system-wide security policies, user restrictions, and OS configurations on a local machine.

terms.name: In-place upgrade
terms.definition: Updating an existing Windows installation to a newer version or edition while keeping all existing files, settings, and installed applications intact.

terms.name: Clean install
terms.definition: Completely wiping the storage drive (formatting) and installing a fresh copy of the operating system from scratch, requiring manually restoring files and reinstalling software.

terms.name: Task Manager
terms.definition: Processes, Performance, Startup, Users, and Services in one place. View all running processes (interactive apps, background tasks, and system processes from other accounts), monitor real-time and historical CPU/memory/disk/network performance, toggle which programs start with sign-in, see who is connected and disconnect them, and start/stop/restart background services.

terms.name: MMC (Custom Console)
terms.definition: Build your own management console from snap-ins. A handy starting point for building your own console: add snap-ins like Event Viewer, Local Users and Groups, Disk Management, Task Scheduler, and more.

terms.name: Event Viewer
terms.definition: Central event consolidation — what happened? Browse Application, Security, Setup, and System logs. Events are categorized as Information, Warning, Error, Critical, Successful Audit, or Failure Audit.

terms.name: Disk Management
terms.definition: Manage disks for individual computers and file servers. View and manage volumes and partitions. Warning: actions here (format, delete volume) can erase data — always keep a backup.

terms.name: Task Scheduler
terms.definition: Schedule an application or script — plan your future. Includes predefined schedules you can click and go. Organize tasks with folders and manage them centrally.

terms.name: Device Manager
terms.definition: View and manage hardware devices and drivers. The OS doesn't know how to talk directly to most hardware — device drivers are hardware- and OS-specific, and older drivers may not work on newer Windows versions.

terms.name: Certificate Manager
terms.definition: View user and trusted certificates — add and remove. Browse certificate stores such as Personal and Trusted Root Certification Authorities.

terms.name: Local Users and Groups
terms.definition: Manage local users (Administrator, Guest, regular users) and groups. Groups include Administrators, Users, Backup Operators, Power Users, and more.

terms.name: Performance Monitor
terms.definition: Gather long-term statistics on OS metrics. Set alerts and automated actions, store statistics, analyze long-term trends, and view built-in reports.

terms.name: Group Policy Editor
terms.definition: Centrally manage users and systems. Local Group Policy Editor manages the local device (gpedit.msc). Group Policy Management Console integrates with Active Directory (gpmc.msc).

terms.name: System Information
terms.definition: System overview: hardware resources, components, software environment. Hardware Resources: memory, DMA, IRQs, conflicts. Components: multimedia, display, input, network. Software Environment: drivers, print jobs, running tasks.

terms.name: Resource Monitor
terms.definition: Detailed real-time view of performance, separated by category. Categories: Overview, CPU, Memory, Disk, and Network.

terms.name: System Configuration
terms.definition: Manage boot processes, startup, services, etc. — one-stop shop. General, Boot, Services, Startup, and Tools tabs let you control how Windows starts.

terms.name: Disk Cleanup
terms.definition: Find unused or unneeded files — a quick way to free up space. Select categories, then click the button to reclaim disk space.

terms.name: Disk Defragment
terms.definition: Move file fragments so they are contiguous to improve read/write time. Not necessary for solid-state drives — Windows won't defrag an SSD. Requires elevated permissions. Command line: defrag C:

terms.name: Registry Editor
terms.definition: The big, huge master database — hierarchical structure used by almost everything. Used by the kernel, device drivers, services, SAM, the user interface, and applications. Always back up your registry before editing.

terms.name: cd / chdir
terms.definition: Change the working directory. Use \\ to separate folders, cd .. to go up one level, and a drive letter (e.g. D:) to switch volumes. cd Documents

terms.name: dir
terms.definition: List the files and subfolders in the current directory, along with sizes and free space on the drive. dir

terms.name: ipconfig
terms.definition: Show TCP/IP adapter info — IP address, subnet mask, default gateway. Add /all for full details like DNS and DHCP servers. ipconfig /all

terms.name: ping
terms.definition: Test whether a host is reachable and measure round-trip time using ICMP. One of the first tools to reach for when troubleshooting connectivity. ping 8.8.8.8

terms.name: netstat
terms.definition: Show active network connections and listening ports. -a shows all connections, -b shows the owning program (needs elevation), -n skips name resolution. netstat -a

terms.name: nslookup
terms.definition: Query DNS servers for name-to-IP (or IP-to-name) records — useful for checking DNS resolution and server responses. nslookup example.com

terms.name: net use
terms.definition: View, connect, or disconnect mapped network drives and shared folders/printers. Run with no arguments to list current connections. net use

terms.name: net user
terms.definition: View, create, or modify local user accounts. Run with no arguments to list all accounts on the machine. net user jsmith

terms.name: tracert
terms.definition: Map the full route a packet takes to a destination, hop by hop, using ICMP TTL-exceeded replies. Some hops may not respond if they filter ICMP. tracert google.com

terms.name: pathping
terms.definition: Combines ping and tracert: first maps the route, then measures round-trip time and packet loss at each hop over time. pathping 192.168.1.1

terms.name: chkdsk
terms.definition: Check a disk for logical file system errors. /f fixes errors found; /r also locates bad sectors and recovers readable data (implies /f). chkdsk /f

terms.name: format
terms.definition: Formats a disk for use with Windows. Destructive — erases all data on the target volume. Be careful. format D: /FS:NTFS

terms.name: diskpart
terms.definition: Opens an interactive disk-partitioning console for managing disks, partitions, and volumes. Destructive if used carelessly. diskpart

terms.name: md
terms.definition: (make directory) Creates a new folder at the specified path. md NewFolder

terms.name: rmdir
terms.definition: (remove directory) Deletes an existing folder. The folder must be empty unless /s is used. rmdir OldFolder

terms.name: robocopy
terms.definition: Robust file/folder copy tool built into Windows — faster and more reliable than copy/paste for large jobs, with retry and logging built in. robocopy C:\\Src D:\\Dst /E

terms.name: hostname
terms.definition: Prints the computer's network name. Handy for telling identical-looking terminal tabs apart. hostname

terms.name: winver
terms.definition: Opens the About Windows dialog showing the OS edition and build number — a quick way to confirm you're on the latest version. winver

terms.name: whoami
terms.definition: Shows the currently logged-in user, and with /all, their group memberships, SID, and privileges. Useful when several accounts are in play. whoami /all

terms.name: [command] /?
terms.definition: Shows built-in help, syntax, and available parameters for almost any command-line tool. robocopy /?

terms.name: gpupdate
terms.definition: Refreshes Group Policy settings on a domain-joined computer without waiting for the normal update cycle. gpupdate /force

terms.name: gpresult
terms.definition: Displays a summary of Group Policy settings that currently apply to the computer and the logged-in user. gpresult /r

terms.name: sfc
terms.definition: System File Checker — scans the integrity of protected Windows system files and repairs corrupted ones when possible. sfc /scannow

terms.name: Internet Options
terms.definition: Configure browser proxy settings, security zones, certificate management, privacy settings, and temporary internet files. Control Panel › Internet Options

terms.name: Devices and Printers
terms.definition: Add peripheral devices, view connected hardware, set default printer, manage print queues, and configure printer properties. Control Panel › Devices and Printers

terms.name: Program and Features
terms.definition: Uninstall desktop applications, view installed updates, and turn optional Windows features on or off. Control Panel › Programs and Features

terms.name: Network and Sharing Center
terms.definition: View network topology, map network drives, change adapter IP or DNS settings, set network profiles, and configure advanced sharing. Control Panel › Network and Sharing Center

terms.name: System (Control Panel)
terms.definition: View basic system specs, rename computer, join Active Directory domain or workgroup, and access System Protection restore points. Control Panel › System

terms.name: Windows Defender Firewall
terms.definition: Configure inbound and outbound traffic rules, allow applications through firewall, enable profiles, and set logging options. Control Panel › Windows Defender Firewall

terms.name: Mail
terms.definition: Set up local email client profiles, configure Exchange, IMAP, or POP3 accounts, and manage data files like PST and OST. Control Panel › Mail

terms.name: Sound
terms.definition: Select default playback and recording audio devices, configure speaker properties, adjust volume, and manage auto-muting. Control Panel › Sound

terms.name: User Accounts
terms.definition: Manage local user profiles, change account types, manage saved Windows credentials, and adjust User Account Control settings. Control Panel › User Accounts

terms.name: Device Manager
terms.definition: View and troubleshoot hardware, update, roll back, or disable drivers, and resolve hardware resource conflicts. Control Panel › Device Manager

terms.name: Indexing Options
terms.definition: Modify search indexing locations and file types to rebuild search catalogs and accelerate File Explorer search. Control Panel › Indexing Options

terms.name: Administrative Tools
terms.definition: Access core management consoles including Computer Management, Event Viewer, Services, Local Security Policy, and Task Scheduler. Control Panel › Administrative Tools

terms.name: File Explorer Options
terms.definition: Configure global settings for file browsing, folder views, search behavior, and hidden file visibility. Control Panel › File Explorer Options

terms.name: File Explorer Options — View hidden files
terms.definition: Select "Show hidden files, folders, and drives" under the View tab to reveal system or hidden items. File Explorer Options › View tab

terms.name: File Explorer Options — Hide extensions
terms.definition: Uncheck "Hide extensions for known file types" to display full file extensions for identifying malware files. File Explorer Options › View tab

terms.name: File Explorer Options — General options
terms.definition: Set default opening location like This PC or Quick Access, clear history, and manage folder opening behavior. File Explorer Options › General tab

terms.name: File Explorer Options — View options
terms.definition: Apply current folder view settings to all folders of the same type, show drive letters, or toggle preview pane. File Explorer Options › View tab

terms.name: Power Options
terms.definition: Manage computer energy usage, sleep behaviors, power plan profiles, and hardware button actions. Control Panel › Power Options

terms.name: Power Options — Hibernate
terms.definition: Saves active system memory to hard drive hiberfil.sys and powers off the system for preserving battery during long downtime. Power Options › Sleep States

terms.name: Power Options — Power plans
terms.definition: Select or customize power profiles like Balanced, Power Saver, or High Performance to balance battery life and system performance. Power Options › Power Plans

terms.name: Power Options — Sleep/suspend
terms.definition: Keeps RAM powered while placing CPU and components into low-power states for fast instant-on resumption. Power Options › Sleep States

terms.name: Power Options — Standby
terms.definition: Legacy low-power state that preserves system session in memory while powering down non-essential hardware. Power Options › Sleep States

terms.name: Power Options — Choose what closing the lid does
terms.definition: Defines hardware button and lid closure actions like Do Nothing, Sleep, Hibernate, or Shut Down. Power Options › System Settings

terms.name: Power Options — Turn on fast startup
terms.definition: Hybrid boot state that saves the Windows kernel session state to disk during shutdown to reduce boot times. Power Options › System Settings

terms.name: Power Options — USB selective suspend
terms.definition: Power-saving feature that suspends power to individual USB ports when idle without affecting other USB devices. Power Options › Advanced Settings

terms.name: Ease of Access
terms.definition: Configure accessibility features including Display scale, Narrator, Magnifier, High Contrast, Sticky Keys, and Mouse pointer size. Control Panel › Ease of Access

terms.name: Time and Language
terms.definition: Set time zone automatically, sync clock servers, add language packs, configure regional formats, and adjust speech or keyboard input. Settings › Time & Language

terms.name: Update and Security
terms.definition: Manage Windows Update schedules, Delivery Optimization, Windows Security Defender, File History Backup, and Reset This PC recovery. Settings › Update & Security

terms.name: Personalization
terms.definition: Customize Desktop background, colors, Lock Screen images, system Themes, Fonts, and Start menu or Taskbar behaviors. Settings › Personalization

terms.name: Apps
terms.definition: Uninstall modern UWP apps and legacy software, set default apps by protocol or file type, and manage startup applications. Settings › Apps

terms.name: Privacy
terms.definition: Control app permissions for hardware like Camera and Microphone, manage background app permissions, and configure diagnostic data. Settings › Privacy

terms.name: System (Settings)
terms.definition: Manage Display resolution, Sound outputs, Notifications, Focus Assist, Storage Sense drive cleanup, and Remote Desktop access. Settings › System

terms.name: Devices (Settings)
terms.definition: Pair Bluetooth devices, add printers or scanners, adjust touchpad sensitivity, and manage USB connection notifications. Settings › Devices

terms.name: Network and Internet
terms.definition: Toggle Wi-Fi or Ethernet, configure VPN connections, set up proxy servers, view Data Usage limits, and perform Network Reset. Settings › Network & Internet

terms.name: Gaming
terms.definition: Configure Xbox Game Bar, adjust Game Mode settings for hardware performance allocation, and manage screen recording options. Settings › Gaming

terms.name: Accounts
terms.definition: Sign in with Microsoft account, manage Work or School connections, set up Windows Hello PIN or biometrics, and manage family accounts. Settings › Accounts

terms.name: Domain joined vs. workgroup
terms.definition: Compares centralized authentication using Active Directory and domain controllers against decentralized peer-to-peer administrative groups. System Properties (sysdm.cpl)

terms.name: Shared resources
terms.definition: Network assets like folders and devices made accessible across the network using NTFS and share permissions. File Explorer → \\\\FS01\\Shared → Properties

terms.name: Printers
terms.definition: Networked printing devices managed centrally via print servers, or shared locally across workgroup computers. Printers & Scanners

terms.name: File servers
terms.definition: Centralized storage systems in a domain environment providing authenticated file shares and access controls. File Explorer → Network → FS01

terms.name: Mapped drives
terms.definition: Mounting network shared folders to a local drive letter for quick access in File Explorer. File Explorer → This PC → Map network drive…

terms.name: Local OS firewall settings
terms.definition: Software-based security rules configured to allow or block inbound and outbound network traffic on a host. Windows Defender Firewall (firewall.cpl)

terms.name: Application restrictions and exceptions
terms.definition: Rules configured to allow specific programs or block executable binaries through network ports. Firewall → Allowed apps

terms.name: Firewall Configuration
terms.definition: Setting firewall profiles like Public, Private, and Domain to enforce distinct traffic filtering rules. Firewall → Home (profiles)

terms.name: Client network configuration
terms.definition: Setting adapter parameters including IP addressing, subnetting, gateway routing, and name resolution. Network Connections → Adapter Properties

terms.name: IP addressing scheme
terms.definition: System of unique logical numbers like IPv4 or IPv6 assigned to network host interfaces. IPv4 Properties → IP address

terms.name: DNS settings
terms.definition: Configured IP addresses of servers that resolve human-readable domain names to IP addresses. IPv4 Properties → DNS servers

terms.name: Subnet mask
terms.definition: A 32-bit mask that separates an IP address into its network ID and host ID portions. IPv4 Properties → Subnet mask

terms.name: Gateway
terms.definition: The IP address of the local router interface that forwards out-of-subnet traffic to external networks. IPv4 Properties → Default gateway

terms.name: Static vs. dynamic
terms.definition: Choosing manually assigned permanent IP settings versus automatic configuration via DHCP. IPv4 Properties → Obtain automatically / Use the following

terms.name: Establish network connections
terms.definition: Configuring local client network adapters to connect to local and remote infrastructure. Settings → Network & Internet

terms.name: Virtual private network (VPN)
terms.definition: Encrypted tunnel created over a public network to provide secure remote access to a private network. Settings → VPN

terms.name: Wireless
terms.definition: Connecting to local area networks using Wi-Fi radio standards and security protocols like WPA3. Settings → Wi-Fi

terms.name: Wired
terms.definition: Physical Ethernet cable connection linking a local network interface card directly to a switch or router port. Settings → Ethernet

terms.name: Wireless wide area network (WWAN)/cellular network
terms.definition: Connecting laptops or mobile devices to internet services using cellular data networks like 4G LTE or 5G. Settings → Mobile hotspot

terms.name: Proxy settings
terms.definition: Redirecting client web traffic through an intermediate proxy server for security inspection, caching, or content filtering. Settings → Proxy

terms.name: Public network vs private network
terms.definition: Network location profiles that automatically adjust firewall rules, hiding the device on public Wi-Fi or enabling discovery on trusted private networks. Settings → Status → Network profile

terms.name: File Explorer navigation – network paths
terms.definition: Accessing shared resources using Universal Naming Convention paths like \\\\ServerName\\ShareName. File Explorer address bar → \\\\ServerName\\ShareName

terms.name: Metered connections and limitations
terms.definition: Setting a data-cap constraint on Wi-Fi or cellular connections to restrict background data usage and defer automatic Windows updates. Settings → Wi-Fi → Properties → Metered connection

terms.name: .dmg
terms.definition: Disk Image file format used to distribute software on macOS. Mounts like a virtual volume containing application installers or bundle folders. Double-click Installer.dmg in Finder

terms.name: .pkg
terms.definition: Installer package format containing an installation wizard, scripts, and payload files used to install software across system directories. Double-click Sample.pkg in Finder

terms.name: .app
terms.definition: Application bundle directory structure in macOS that appears as a single executable file to the end user. Finder → Applications

terms.name: App Store
terms.definition: Official Apple digital distribution platform for discovering, purchasing, and securely downloading vetted macOS applications. Open App Store

terms.name: Uninstallation Process
terms.definition: Removal method for macOS apps — typically dragging a .app bundle from /Applications to the Trash, or running a dedicated uninstaller script for .pkg-installed software. Select an app in Applications, then Move to Trash

terms.name: /Applications
terms.definition: Root directory storing installed applications accessible to all system users. Finder → /Applications

terms.name: /Users
terms.definition: System folder containing individual user profile directories, including home folders, personal data, and desktop configurations. Finder → /Users

terms.name: /Library
terms.definition: System-wide configuration folder storing shared application support files, drivers, and global preferences accessible by all users. Finder → /Library

terms.name: /System
terms.definition: Core OS directory containing critical macOS operating system files, system frameworks, and kernel components protected by System Integrity Protection (SIP). Finder → /System

terms.name: ~/Library
terms.definition: User-specific Library folder (at /Users/<name>/Library) containing individual app preferences, caches, application support files, and user data. Finder → Users/jsmith/Library

terms.name: Apple ID and Corporate Restrictions
terms.definition: Identity management for Apple services that organizations can manage via Mobile Device Management (MDM) enrollment profiles to enforce security policies and restrict features. System Settings → Apple ID

terms.name: Backups
terms.definition: Best practice of using utilities like Time Machine or third-party tools to maintain regular data copies on external or network drives. Open Time Machine

terms.name: Antivirus
terms.definition: Security best practice of running endpoint protection or relying on built-in macOS security layers (XProtect, MRT) to detect and block malicious software. System Settings → Privacy & Security

terms.name: Updates/Patches
terms.definition: Routine operating system and application updates deployed via System Settings to resolve vulnerabilities, fix bugs, and optimize system performance. System Settings → General

terms.name: Rapid Security Response (RSR)
terms.definition: Automated macOS security mechanism delivering critical security fixes between standard software updates, without requiring a full OS reboot. System Settings → General

terms.name: Displays
terms.definition: System Settings pane used to adjust screen resolution, arrangement, orientation, color profiles, and relative placement in multi-monitor setups. System Settings → Displays

terms.name: Networks
terms.definition: System Settings menu for managing network adapters, Wi-Fi connections, Ethernet interfaces, IPv4/IPv6 settings, DNS configuration, and proxies. System Settings → Network

terms.name: Printers & Scanners
terms.definition: System interface for adding, configuring, sharing, and troubleshooting printing and scanning hardware on local or network connections. System Settings → Printers & Scanners

terms.name: Privacy
terms.definition: System Settings pane for managing per-application permissions to device sensors and user data, including Location Services, Camera, Microphone, and Contacts. System Settings → Privacy & Security

terms.name: Accessibility
terms.definition: System Settings menu providing custom input and display options for accessibility, plus permissions for apps needing system-level control and automation. System Settings → Accessibility

terms.name: Time Machine
terms.definition: Automated macOS backup feature that maintains hourly snapshots for 24 hours, daily backups for a month, and weekly backups for prior months. Open Time Machine

terms.name: Multiple Desktops
terms.definition: Feature allowing users to create separate virtual workspace environments ("Spaces") to organize open application windows. Mission Control (Control+↑)

terms.name: Mission Control
terms.definition: Window management interface launched via trackpad gestures or Control+Up Arrow that displays all open windows, full-screen apps, and virtual desktop Spaces. Trigger Mission Control (Control+↑)

terms.name: Keychain
terms.definition: Encrypted password management database in macOS that securely stores user passwords, certificates, keys, and private application credentials, unlocked via login. Open Keychain Access

terms.name: Spotlight
terms.definition: System-wide indexing and search utility launched via Command+Space to locate local files, launch applications, perform calculations, and fetch web data. Trigger Spotlight (⌘+Space)

terms.name: iCloud
terms.definition: Apple cloud storage and synchronization infrastructure that links user data across macOS, iOS, and iPadOS devices. See it via Apple ID pane

terms.name: iMessage
terms.definition: Messaging service integrated into the macOS Messages application for secure text, media, and data communication across Apple devices. Concept — no simulated app

terms.name: FaceTime
terms.definition: Built-in audio and video conferencing application integrated with macOS and iOS. Concept — no simulated app

terms.name: iCloud Drive
terms.definition: Cloud-based file storage and synchronization folder built into the macOS file system, similar to Google Drive or Dropbox. Finder → iCloud Drive

terms.name: Gestures
terms.definition: Multi-touch trackpad and mouse input shortcuts allowing users to navigate, swipe, pinch, or tap to trigger system functions like Mission Control or desktop switching. Concept — trackpad input

terms.name: Finder
terms.definition: Primary macOS desktop file manager used to browse, organize, launch, rename, and manage files, network shares, and connected media. Open Finder

terms.name: Dock
terms.definition: Desktop shortcut bar providing quick access to pinned apps, open applications (indicated by a dot below the icon), folders, and the Trash. Look at the bottom of the screen

terms.name: Continuity
terms.definition: Ecosystem integration allowing Apple devices to share features seamlessly, such as using an iPhone as a Mac webcam, AirDrop file sharing, and Universal Clipboard. Concept — cross-device features

terms.name: Disk Utility
terms.definition: System administration utility used to format, partition, repair (First Aid), erase, and create disk images of local storage drives and volumes. Open Disk Utility

terms.name: FileVault
terms.definition: Built-in macOS Full Disk Encryption (FDE) feature that protects system drive data using AES encryption linked to user credentials or a recovery key. System Settings → Privacy & Security

terms.name: Terminal
terms.definition: Command-line interface application providing shell access (zsh/bash) for file manipulation, system configuration, scripting, and administrative functions. Open Terminal

terms.name: Force Quit
terms.definition: Troubleshooting feature (Command+Option+Escape) used to immediately terminate non-responsive or malfunctioning applications. ⌘+Option+Esc

terms.name: ls
terms.definition: Command used to list files and directory contents within the current or specified path. ls -la

terms.name: pwd
terms.definition: Print Working Directory command that outputs the full absolute path of the current directory. pwd

terms.name: mv
terms.definition: Command used to move files or directories, as well as rename them. mv notes.txt Documents/

terms.name: cp
terms.definition: Command used to copy files and directories from a source location to a destination. cp -r Documents Documents_backup

terms.name: rm
terms.definition: Command used to remove or delete files and directories permanently from the filesystem. rm -r Downloads

terms.name: chmod
terms.definition: Change Mode command used to modify file and directory read, write, and execute permissions. chmod 755 project/app.py

terms.name: chown
terms.definition: Change Owner command used to modify the user and/or group ownership of files and directories. sudo chown jsmith:jsmith notes.txt

terms.name: grep
terms.definition: Global Regular Expression Print command used to search for specific text or patterns within files or command output. grep -in error /var/log/syslog

terms.name: find
terms.definition: Search utility used to locate files and directories within a directory hierarchy based on criteria like name, size, or permissions. find /home/jsmith -name "*.txt"

terms.name: fsck
terms.definition: File System Check utility used to inspect, repair, and report errors on Linux filesystems. sudo fsck -f /dev/sda1

terms.name: mount
terms.definition: Command used to attach external storage devices, partitions, or network shares to a designated point in the directory tree. mount

terms.name: su
terms.definition: Switch User utility used to change the current terminal session identity to another user account or the root account. su -

terms.name: sudo
terms.definition: Superuser Do command allowing authorized users to execute specific commands with elevated security permissions. sudo apt update

terms.name: apt
terms.definition: Advanced Package Tool used on Debian-based distributions (like Ubuntu) to install, update, upgrade, and remove software packages. sudo apt install htop

terms.name: dnf
terms.definition: Dandified YUM package manager used on Red Hat-based distributions (like Fedora and RHEL) to manage software installations and dependencies. sudo dnf install htop

terms.name: ip
terms.definition: Modern network configuration utility used to manage network interfaces, routing tables, and IP addresses. ip addr

terms.name: ping
terms.definition: Network utility that sends ICMP Echo Request packets to a destination to test basic reachability and latency. ping -c 4 8.8.8.8

terms.name: curl
terms.definition: Command-line tool used to transfer data to or from a server using protocols like HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and SFTP. curl -I https://example.com

terms.name: dig
terms.definition: Domain Information Groper utility used to query DNS name servers for troubleshooting domain resolution and record lookups. dig example.com

terms.name: traceroute
terms.definition: Network diagnostic tool that tracks and displays the path (hops) packets take to reach a destination address. traceroute example.com

terms.name: man
terms.definition: System manual page viewer providing detailed documentation, usage flags, and syntax examples for Linux commands. man grep

terms.name: cat
terms.definition: Concatenate command used to view file contents, combine multiple files, or create new files directly in the terminal. cat /etc/hosts

terms.name: top
terms.definition: Real-time process monitor that displays system resource usage, CPU load, memory consumption, and active processes. top

terms.name: ps
terms.definition: Process Status command that snapshot-reports currently running processes, their Process IDs (PIDs), and resource usage. ps aux

terms.name: du
terms.definition: Disk Usage command used to estimate and display disk space consumed by specific files or directories. du -sh Documents

terms.name: df
terms.definition: Disk Free command that displays total, used, and available space on mounted filesystems. df -h

terms.name: nano
terms.definition: User-friendly, terminal-based text editor commonly used for quick configuration edits without complex modal modes. nano Documents/notes.txt

terms.name: /etc/passwd
terms.definition: Local system file storing user account information, including user IDs (UID), group IDs (GID), home directories, and default shells. cat /etc/passwd

terms.name: /etc/shadow
terms.definition: Secured system file accessible only by root that stores encrypted user account passwords and password aging policies. sudo cat /etc/shadow

terms.name: /etc/hosts
terms.definition: Static lookup table used to map hostnames directly to IP addresses locally before querying DNS servers. cat /etc/hosts

terms.name: /etc/fstab
terms.definition: Filesystem table configuration file that defines static file system mounts, partitions, and options applied at system boot. cat /etc/fstab

terms.name: /etc/resolv.conf
terms.definition: System configuration file containing local DNS server addresses and search domain preferences. cat /etc/resolv.conf

terms.name: systemd
terms.definition: Primary system and service manager for modern Linux OSs that initializes user space, boots the OS, and manages system processes. man systemd

terms.name: kernel
terms.definition: Core component of the Linux operating system that manages hardware resources, system memory, CPU cycles, and low-level device drivers. uname -a

terms.name: bootloader
terms.definition: Software program (such as GRUB) that loads the Linux kernel into system memory during the initial boot sequence. man man

terms.name: Root Account
terms.definition: Superuser account on a Linux system possessing unrestricted system privileges and administrative authority. sudo -i

terms.name: 32-bit vs. 64-bit dependent application requirements
terms.definition: System Requirements: Hardware drivers are specific to the OS version — 32-bit (x86) or 64-bit (x64). A 32-bit OS cannot run 64-bit apps. A 64-bit OS can run 32-bit apps.

terms.name: Dedicated vs. integrated graphics card
terms.definition: System Requirements: Integrated: CPU and GPU are the same chip and share system memory for graphics — common in laptops. Dedicated (discrete): has its own VRAM, for high-end graphics requirements.

terms.name: Video random-access memory (VRAM) requirements
terms.definition: System Requirements: VRAM is high-speed memory dedicated exclusively to storing graphical assets — framebuffers, 3D geometry, textures, and depth buffers. Dedicated cards have built-in VRAM; integrated graphics borrow a portion of main system RAM, reducing what is left for other applications.

terms.name: RAM requirements
terms.definition: System Requirements: A critical specification — the application may perform poorly or not at all without enough RAM. This is above and beyond the OS requirements, depends on the application, and must account for every other running application.

terms.name: Central processing unit (CPU) requirements
terms.definition: System Requirements: Processing speed is usually measured in gigahertz (GHz) — a broad measurement where higher numbers mean faster CPUs. Requirements vary a lot by application: word processing needs far less than video editing.

terms.name: External hardware tokens
terms.definition: System Requirements: Used to manage application usage and limit access to authorized users — the application will only operate with the hardware token connected. Commonly a USB device. Can be a challenge to manage, and is often used with high-end software that carries high per-seat licensing costs.

terms.name: Storage requirements
terms.definition: System Requirements: A drive-space concern with two parts: the initial installation space requirement, and ongoing application-use requirements. Some applications consume a lot of additional storage after installation — so the initial install size may not be the most important number.

terms.name: Application to OS compatibility
terms.definition: System Requirements: The software must match the system architecture (32-bit vs. 64-bit), have its software dependencies satisfied, and meet the operating system API requirements of the host environment in order to run properly.

terms.name: Physical media vs. mountable ISO file
terms.definition: Deployment Methods: Physical media — optical disc, USB drive, etc. — is increasingly rare. An ISO is an optical disk image: a single file that is a sector-by-sector copy of a disc's files and folders, which can be mounted directly.

terms.name: Downloadable package
terms.definition: Deployment Methods: Get the installer direct from the manufacturer or a centralized app store — and avoid third-party download sites, which carry a higher risk of tampered or bundled software.

terms.name: Image deployment
terms.definition: Deployment Methods: Create a standard OS "master image" (gold image) and clone it across many target systems over the network or via physical media. A perfect fit for virtual machines, and very fast to deploy at scale.

terms.name: Device impact considerations for new applications
terms.definition: Impact Considerations: Think through what a new application or upgrade can do to the device it runs on: it may stop working after an upgrade, cause slowdowns, or even delete files.

terms.name: Network impact considerations for new applications
terms.definition: Impact Considerations: A new application often needs access to internal services, plus the rights and permissions to reach file shares — both of which need to be planned and provisioned.

terms.name: Operation impact considerations for new applications
terms.definition: Impact Considerations: Many jobs are time-sensitive. An updated application may require a change to an existing workflow — or it may not work with that workflow at all.

terms.name: Business impact considerations for new applications
terms.definition: Impact Considerations: Critical business processes are sensitive to downtime and outages. A change to one application can create issues elsewhere — other parts of the business rely on its results.

terms.name: Email Systems
terms.definition: Cloud-based communication infrastructure (e.g., Exchange Online, Gmail) providing business email hosting, domain routing, MX record configuration, and mailbox setup. Outlook → Mail flow (MX records)

terms.name: Cloud Storage
terms.definition: Centralized online repositories (e.g., OneDrive, Google Drive) enabling secure file storage, file sharing permissions, version control, and cloud accessibility. Open OneDrive

terms.name: Sync and Folder Settings
terms.definition: Configuration rules controlling how local directories synchronize with cloud storage, including selective sync, bandwidth limits, and sync options. OneDrive → Sync settings

terms.name: Collaboration Tools
terms.definition: Integrated cloud application suites designed for multi-user real-time document editing, project management, and team communication. Open Teams

terms.name: Spreadsheets
terms.definition: Cloud-based data tools (e.g., Excel Online, Google Sheets) enabling multi-user data analysis, simultaneous cell editing, automated calculations, and live version tracking. Open Excel Online

terms.name: Videoconferencing
terms.definition: Real-time virtual meeting software (e.g., Microsoft Teams, Zoom, Google Meet) facilitating remote video calls, screen sharing, meeting recordings, and breakout rooms. Teams → Meet now

terms.name: Presentation Tools
terms.definition: Cloud applications (e.g., PowerPoint Online, Google Slides) allowing teams to remotely co-author, present, and update digital slide decks. Open PowerPoint Online

terms.name: Word Processing Tools
terms.definition: Online document platforms (e.g., Word Online, Google Docs) allowing multiple users to edit text, leave inline comments, and track changes in real time. Open Word Online

terms.name: Instant Messaging
terms.definition: Real-time chat systems (e.g., Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Chat) providing direct messaging, topic-based channels, file attachments, and status indicators. Teams → Chat

terms.name: Identity Synchronization
terms.definition: Process of mirroring local Active Directory users and credentials to cloud identity providers (e.g., Entra ID Connect) for single sign-on (SSO) and hybrid user access. Admin Center → Identity

terms.name: Licensing Assignment
terms.definition: Administrative process of provisioning, purchasing, and revoking subscription licenses (e.g., Microsoft 365, Google Workspace) to managed user accounts. Admin Center → Licenses
